chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Makes a Stock Cyclical or Defensive

lessons.title: Moving Targets: When Defensives Turn Cyclical and Cyclicals Turn Defensive

body.text: A classification is a snapshot of a business, not a permanent tag. Industries consolidate, balance sheets change, companies split, and regulators step in. The label you gave a stock five years ago may be quietly wrong today.

children.text: The measurement routine from the last lesson looks backwards. It tells you how a business behaved over the past decade. That is the right starting point, but it carries a hidden assumption: that the business will keep behaving the same way. This lesson is about when that assumption fails, and how to catch the shift before the market does.
Case 1: Indian Telecom, From Stable to Brutal and Back

On paper, telecom looks like a textbook defensive. Hundreds of millions of people pay a monthly bill whether GDP grows at 8% or 4%. Yet for Bharti Airtel shareholders, the late 2010s were anything but defensive. Nothing about the economy caused it. The industry structure did.

body.title: How Industry Structure Moved Telecom Along the Spectrum

events.title: Crowded but stable
events.description: More than half a dozen private operators competed, but pricing was rational enough for leaders like Bharti Airtel to earn steady profits.

events.title: Reliance Jio launches
events.description: Free voice and very cheap data trigger a price war. Industry revenue per user falls sharply and weaker operators start exiting or merging.

events.title: Consolidation under pressure
events.description: Vodafone and Idea merge, several smaller operators shut down or sell out. Airtel's profits shrink dramatically despite a growing subscriber base.

events.title: AGR ruling
events.description: The Supreme Court's adjusted gross revenue ruling creates large past dues for operators, and Airtel reports a heavy loss for FY20.

events.title: Tariff hikes return
events.description: With effectively three private players left, the industry raises tariffs in rounds, including December 2019, late 2021, and mid 2024. Earnings stability starts returning.

body.text: The lesson from telecom: demand stability alone does not make a business defensive. Pricing power does. A necessity product sold in a price war behaves like a deep cyclical. The same product sold by three rational players behaves like a defensive.

children.text: Case 2: Indian IT, the Defensive That Wasn't Quite

For years, Indian IT services stocks were treated as a safe haven: debt-free balance sheets, dollar revenues that benefit when the rupee weakens, and generous dividends and buybacks. Then the post-pandemic cycle exposed the other side. Clients rushed to spend on digital projects in FY22, then cut discretionary technology budgets as US interest rates rose, and growth at the largest companies slowed to low single digits by FY24. Profits held up, so IT did not become a deep cyclical. But investors who had filed it next to FMCG learned that its growth depends heavily on the global business cycle, which places it firmly in the quasi-defensive band.
Case 3: Demergers Can Change the Label Overnight

A conglomerate's classification is a weighted blend of its businesses. ITC is the Indian example most investors know: a highly stable cigarettes and FMCG engine alongside hotels, paperboards, and agri-business, which are far more sensitive to the economy. When ITC demerged its hotels business into ITC Hotels, which listed in January 2025, the remaining company became a little more defensive, while ITC Hotels shareholders took on a pure travel-and-hospitality cyclical. Same investors, different risk, by corporate action alone.

body.caption: Illustrative conglomerate DiversiCo: segment operating profit, ₹ crore

body.title: Recalculate After the Demerger
body.prompt: DiversiCo demerges its hotels segment into a separate listed company. What share of the remaining company's operating profit now comes from the true defensive staples segment? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Remaining operating profit = 10,000 - 1,000 = ₹9,000 crore. Staples share = 6,000 / 9,000 × 100 = 66.7%, up from 60%. Removing one cyclical segment moved the whole company further towards the defensive end without any change in how its staples business behaves.

children.text: Five Forces That Move a Company Along the Spectrum

body.caption: What to watch, and which way it pushes

cells: Players consolidate and pricing becomes rational
A new entrant or overcapacity sparks a price war
Telecom after Jio, then after consolidation
Debt is repaid, so interest no longer amplifies downturns
Debt-funded expansion raises fixed interest costs
Metal and infrastructure companies that deleveraged after the 2010s bad loan cycle
Cyclical segments are sold or demerged
The company enters capital-heavy or commodity businesses
Revenue shifts to many small, recurring customers
Revenue concentrates in a few large or capex-driven clients
Private banks shifting loan books from large corporates to retail
Returns are fixed by a regulator on a stable formula
Price controls or policy changes cap or disrupt earnings
Regulated returns for Power Grid; drug price controls for some pharma products

body.title: Spot the Shift
body.question: A steel company has spent five years cutting its net debt by more than half and has signed long-term supply contracts with auto makers. Nothing else has changed. What is the most accurate description of the effect?
options: It is now a true defensive
It is still cyclical, but its profits should swing less than before
Nothing changes, because steel prices still drive its revenue
It is now a late cyclical instead of a deep cyclical
body.explanation: Lower debt reduces the financial leverage that turns small operating dips into losses, and contracts smooth some volume. But steel prices are still set by global markets, so the business stays cyclical. It moves along the spectrum, it does not jump to the other end.

children.text: The Most Expensive Mistake: Confusing Structural Decline With a Cyclical Dip

When a defensive company's profits fall, the comforting story is that it is a temporary blip and the cycle will turn. Sometimes that is true. Sometimes the business has permanently lost pricing power to a new competitor, a technology shift, or a regulation, and the old margins are never coming back. Cyclical dips reverse on their own. Structural declines do not, and averaging down into one is how defensive portfolios lose real money.

columns.label: Cyclical dip
points: Most companies in the industry are hurting at the same time
Cause is demand, commodity prices, or rates, which move in cycles
Margins recover once the cycle turns

columns.label: Structural decline
points: One company or model is hurting while a new competitor gains
Market share is steadily lost, quarter after quarter
Cause is competition, disruption, or permanent regulation
Margins stay lower even when the economy improves

body.title: Blip or Break?
body.scenario: Nisha, a mutual fund investor who also holds a few stocks directly, owns a paint company she has always thought of as defensive. Over the last six quarters its volume growth has slowed and margins have fallen by several percentage points. The management blames 'weak urban demand'. At the same time, a large new entrant backed by a cement and chemicals conglomerate has been adding dealers aggressively and offering higher dealer discounts, and two smaller listed peers report rising market share.
body.prompt: Is this more likely a cyclical dip or a structural shift? What should Nisha check before deciding to average down?
body.modelAnswer: The evidence leans towards a structural shift. Weak urban demand would hurt all paint companies, but here peers and a new entrant are gaining while this company loses share and cuts margins, which points to competition, not the cycle. Nisha should check: whether industry volumes are actually falling or just this company's; market share trends over several quarters; whether dealer discounts and advertising spend are rising, a sign of a price war; and what management says about competition in earnings calls, not just demand. If the pressure is competitive, the old margins may not return, and the stock's historical valuation premium may not be a reliable guide.

body.label: Re-check frequency
body.value: Once a year, and after every major event
body.context: Re-run your classification after annual results, and immediately after a demerger, a large acquisition, a new competitor, or a major regulatory change

body.title: Annual Classification Review
steps: Re-run the earnings volatility scorecard with the latest year of data from Screener.in
Check whether the number of serious competitors has increased or decreased
Compare net debt today with three years ago
Read the annual report's segment information for changes in business mix
Scan the last four earnings call transcripts for new competition, pricing pressure, or regulation
Check market share trends to separate cyclical weakness from structural loss
Update the stock's spectrum position and note what changed

cards.definition: What happens to a company's profits, not its share price, when the economy slows.
A business whose growth slows in a downturn but whose profits rarely fall much, such as IT services, pharma, and telecom.
Standard deviation of annual net profit divided by average net profit; higher values indicate more volatile earnings.
The ability to raise prices without losing much volume; the real source of defensiveness, more than stable demand alone.
A permanent loss of margins or market share from competition, disruption, or regulation, which does not reverse when the economic cycle turns.

points: Cyclical and defensive labels describe a business at a point in time and can change
Industry structure matters as much as demand: telecom behaved like a cyclical during its price war and more like a defensive after consolidation
IT services proved to be quasi-defensive, with growth tied to global client budgets even though profits held
Demergers, debt reduction, customer mix, and regulation can all move a company along the spectrum
Separate cyclical dips, which reverse, from structural declines, which do not, before averaging down
Re-check every classification at least once a year and after any major corporate or industry event

body.text: DiversiCo, Nisha, and the paint company scenario are illustrative. Descriptions of Bharti Airtel, Indian IT services, and ITC summarise publicly reported developments for education; check company filings for exact figures and dates. Nothing in this lesson is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
